title: Diagnostic and Remedial Teaching
description: Comprehensive shared preparation notes and worked practice for Diagnostic and Remedial Teaching. Review the target examination syllabus and level before reuse.

coverage: Distinguish procedural slips from conceptual barriers
Use concrete, visual and symbolic scaffolds
Monitor progress and adapt or fade support

sections.label: Concepts and worked examples
sections.html:
Diagnose before intervening

Remedial teaching responds to a specific learning need. Use a brief diagnostic task, interview or work sample to locate the missing prerequisite and determine whether the barrier is conceptual, procedural, linguistic or related to confidence and access.

Targeted teaching cycle

Set a small observable goal, connect to what the learner knows, model one strategy, guide practice with feedback, then provide independent practice. Move between concrete, pictorial and symbolic representations and explicitly connect them.

Monitor and adjust

Use frequent low-stakes checks on fresh examples. If progress stalls, revisit the diagnosis or change the representation, examples or amount of scaffolding. Fade support when the learner can select and use the strategy independently.

Worked intervention example: If a student subtracts fractions by subtracting both numerators and denominators, first check whether the student understands equal-sized parts. Use same-size fraction strips to rename (\(3/4-1/2\)) as (\(3/4-2/4\)), then connect the model to the common-denominator procedure.

sections.label: Methods and exam checks
sections.html:
• Teach the prerequisite gap, not a long list of unrelated exercises.
  • Ask the learner to think aloud to expose the strategy being used.
  • Use worked examples followed by partially completed examples and then independent tasks.
  • Provide enough varied practice to test transfer, not only repetition of one item.
  • Set a review date and use progress evidence to fade or revise support.

sections.label: Key facts and formulas
sections.html:
• Remediation is targeted support, not punishment or simply assigning more of the same work.
  • Scaffolding should support success while preserving meaningful student thinking.
  • Concrete materials are most useful when their features map clearly to the mathematical idea.
  • Progress monitoring checks whether the intervention is working for this learner.

sections.label: Worked practice
sections.html:
1. Core:

    Several learners make errors adding fractions with unlike denominators. What should the teacher do first?

    1. Assign harder fraction sums
    2. Diagnose understanding of equivalent fractions and common denominators
    3. Remove all fraction work
    4. Give the same explanation louder
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: Diagnose understanding of equivalent fractions and common denominators

    The teacher should locate the prerequisite gap before planning targeted instruction.

  2. Core:

    After targeted instruction, what best checks whether the support worked?

    1. A new problem testing the same skill independently
    2. Repeating the original lecture only
    3. A spelling quiz
    4. No follow-up
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: A new problem testing the same skill independently

    An independent, aligned problem provides evidence of whether the learner can now use the skill.

  3. Foundation:

    A student repeatedly adds denominators when adding fractions. What should the teacher do first?

    1. Assign 50 more problems immediately
    2. Diagnose the student's understanding of equal-sized fractional parts
    3. Remove fractions from the course
    4. Teach decimal multiplication instead
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: Diagnose the student's understanding of equal-sized fractional parts

    The error suggests a conceptual issue about units and equivalent parts. Diagnose the reasoning before selecting an intervention.

  4. Standard:

    Which sequence best supports a learner who cannot yet subtract unlike fractions?

    1. Abstract rule, timed test, then no feedback
    2. Fraction strips, matching visual partitions, symbolic common-denominator work
    3. Memorise answers, skip models, increase speed
    4. Use unrelated geometry examples
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: Fraction strips, matching visual partitions, symbolic common-denominator work

    The sequence connects a concrete model to a visual representation and then to symbols.

  5. Challenge:

    When should a scaffold be faded?

    1. As soon as the teacher has modelled once
    2. When evidence shows the learner can perform the target independently across suitable examples
    3. Only at the end of the school year
    4. Never, because support should remain identical
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: When evidence shows the learner can perform the target independently across suitable examples

    Fading follows demonstrated independence and transfer, while monitoring continues for retention.
